content.body: Have you ever typed a message, used backspace, and wondered if the final text matches what someone else typed? That's exactly what we're solving today. We'll learn how to compare two strings after applying backspace operations efficiently.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply a single-pass approach to process backspaces
• Implement a helper function using a stack-like structure
• Explain why this approach is more efficient than brute force reconstruction
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple example. Given two strings with '#' representing backspace, can you tell if they become the same?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: Do 'ab#c' and 'ad#c' become the same after applying backspaces?

content.title: Try a longer example
content.successMessage: Well done! Both become 'c' after processing all backspaces.

content.title: One more challenge
content.successMessage: Great! You manually tracked backspaces to see both become 'xywrrmp'.

content.body: What you just did was manual reconstruction: you mentally processed each character and backspace to rebuild the strings, then compared them. This works for short examples but becomes tedious for long strings.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When strings have thousands of characters with many backspaces, manually rebuilding both strings completely before comparing is inefficient. We need a smarter approach that processes characters just once. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of reconstructing entire strings, we can process characters in one pass while using a simple structure to track the result so far. For backspace problems, we need a way to easily remove the last character we added - like using a notebook where we write characters but can erase the last entry with one step.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll process each string separately using a helper function that simulates typing with backspace. The key insight: we can use an array as a stack to build the result character by character.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Processing 'ab#c': Start with empty array [].
• Read 'a' → push → ['a']
• Read 'b' → push → ['a','b']
• Read '#' → pop → ['a']
• Read 'c' → push → ['a','c']
Result: 'ac'

Processing 'ad#c':
• 'a' → ['a']
• 'd' → ['a','d']
• '#' → ['a']
• 'c' → ['a','c']
Both give 'ac', so they match!

content.body:
1. Create a helper function that processes a string with backspaces
2. Use an array to build the result character by character
3. When we see '#', remove the last character if there is one
4. Compare the processed results of both strings
5. Return true if they match, false otherwise
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the helper function skeleton
steps.instruction: Start by creating a function called 'processString' that takes one parameter 'str'. We'll implement the backspace logic inside it.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've created the function skeleton.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you have the function keyword, name 'processString', and parameter 'str'.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. We need a function named processString that accepts one parameter called str.

steps.title: Initialize the result array
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create an empty array called 'result' that will store our processed characters.
steps.hint: Use const result = []; inside the function body.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! The result array is ready to store characters.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close. Make sure you're declaring 'result' as a constant and initializing it as an empty array.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to create an array variable called 'result' inside the function.

steps.title: Loop through the string
steps.instruction: Add a for loop to iterate through each character of the input string. We'll process one character at a time.
steps.hint: Use for (let i = 0; i < str.length; i++) { }
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now we can process each character in the string.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Check your loop syntax - we need to iterate from 0 to str.length.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need a for loop that goes through each character index in the string.

steps.title: Handle regular characters and backspaces
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, check if the current character is '#'. If it is, remove the last character from result (if any). Otherwise, add the character to result.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now the function correctly processes backspaces and regular characters.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you're checking for '#' and using pop() for backspace, push() for regular characters.

steps.title: Return the processed string and implement main function
steps.instruction: After the loop, return result joined as a string. Then create the main function backspaceCompare that uses processString on both inputs and compares them.
steps.hint: Add return result.join(''); at the end of processString, then implement backspaceCompare.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've successfully implemented the complete solution.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Don't forget to return the joined string from processString and implement backspaceCompare.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to return the processed string and create a function that compares both processed results.

content.body: Great work! You've learned how to efficiently compare strings with backspaces using a single-pass approach. Remember: the key insight was using an array as a stack to build the result incrementally, removing characters when we encounter backspaces. This approach processes each character only once, making it much more efficient than reconstructing entire strings separately.
